spoken: By an oasis in the Tunisian desert stands a stone column for soldiers from Chad.
On a hill near Mareth, concrete bunkers still face south-east.
Near Enfeeda, a village sits on a rock that soldiers climbed at dawn.
The war of 1942 and 1943 left traces like these all over Tunisia. Let's follow them.
In 1942, Tunisia was a French protectorate, ruled in name by the Bey of Tunis.
In November, the Allies landed in Morocco and Algeria, and Germany and Italy rushed troops into Tunis.
Allied armies closed in from the west and from Libya, with soldiers from many nations.
Tunisians of every faith, Muslims, Jews and Christians, lived through the occupation and the fighting.
It ended on 13 May 1943, when the last Axis forces in Africa surrendered.
Our trail runs from south to north, some 500 kilometres as the crow flies.
At each stop, we ask what happened, what you see today, and how to read it on the spot.
Our first stop is Kuh-sar Ghee-lahn, an oasis on the edge of Tunisia's great sea of dunes.
In February 1943, Force L arrived. They were General Luh-clair's Free French, with colonial troops from Chad.
Fort-Lamy, then Chad's capital, lies some 2,400 kilometres away as the crow flies. Here they guarded the Eighth Army's desert flank.
On 10 March, a German armoured group attacked. Allied aircraft struck it, some flown by Australians, and the attack failed.
Today visitors come for the dunes and a warm spring, and near the palms stands Tisavar, a Roman fort.
About a kilometre east of the fighting stands the steely, known here as General Luh-clair's column.
Read the two together. Both mark a desert frontier, and they are at least 1,750 years apart.
One caution. France's travel advice warns against desert areas, so check it before planning this stop.
Some 90 kilometres north-east, near Mareth, a museum stands on a hill.
It explains the Mareth Line, which France built from 1936 to 1940 against an attack from Italian Libya.
It ran 40 to 50 kilometres from the sea to the hills, with 40 infantry casemates, 8 for artillery and 15 command posts.
Disarmed after France's defeat in 1940, it was rearmed by the Axis in late 1942.
On 20 March 1943, the Eighth Army attacked across the wadi, against Italian and German troops, and was thrown back.
Meanwhile, New Zealanders and Force L had gone some 200 kilometres round the hills, to the Tebaga Gap.
They broke through on 26 March, and two days later the Axis was pulling back north.
Today the museum, run by the defence ministry, shows maps, photographs and uniforms, with guns and casemates outside.
Find a casemate's firing slit. It looks south-east, towards Medenine and Libya, where the enemy was expected.
In April, the Axis fell back north, to the hills around Enfeeda.
Five kilometres from the town, the village of Takroona sits on a rocky hill that rises to about 200 metres.
Italian troops held it, with a German company. On the night of 19 April, the New Zealand Division attacked.
At dawn, Lance-Sergeant Hahneh Manahi of the 28th Maori Battalion led a few men up the cliff to a ledge.
On 21 April, a counter-attack retook the ledge. Manahi helped win it back, and then the village.
Four generals backed him for the Victoria Cross, but London gave him a lesser medal.
In 2007, his sons received a sword and a letter from Queen Elizabeth the Second.
Today you climb on foot, past stone houses with vaulted rooms. Only a few families still live here.
Near the top is the shrine of Sidi Abdelkader, and the plain runs east to the sea.
Step back from the summit's edge, and the cliff drops out of sight. Steep ground hides its own foot.
In Enfeeda, the Commonwealth war cemetery holds 1,551 graves, most from the last battles of 1943.
In Hamma-met, 40 kilometres north-east, a white villa stands in a garden by the sea, Dar Sebastian.
George Sebastian, born in Romania, had it built around 1930.
Today it is a cultural centre, whose open-air theatre President Habib Bourguiba opened in 1964.
Guides often say that Rommel stayed here, or even made it his headquarters.
Hatem Bourial, a Tunisian writer who has told its history, says the German army requisitioned it.
Of Rommel, he writes only that he may have spent a few nights here.
Now check the dates. Rommel took overall command in Tunisia on 23 February 1943, and left Africa for good on 9 March.
So the story fits only a few weeks, and none of these sources cites a wartime document.
Nor does the tale of Winston Churchill writing his memoirs here.
Enjoy the house and its garden, and weigh each war story. Ask who tells it, when, and from what evidence.
Our last stop lies 100 kilometres north-west, near Medjez el Bab.
Here a ridge with two summits, Djebel el Ahmera and Djebel Rhar, rises over the Medjerda valley.
British soldiers called it Longstop Hill, after the cricket fielder who stands far behind the wicketkeeper.
Like a long stop, it was the last great barrier on the road to Tunis.
The Coldstream Guards took it in the rain on 22 December 1942, but German counter-attacks drove the Allies off by Christmas Day.
The Germans called it Christmas Hill, and the Allied push on Tunis stopped for four months.
In April 1943, the British 78th Division attacked again, and the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders took Djebel el Ahmera.
Their leader, Major John Anderson, received the Victoria Cross. On the 7th of May, Allied troops entered Tunis.
Today you see the ridge from the road north of Medjez el Bab. Ask locally before walking up.
In the town is Tunisia's largest Commonwealth war cemetery, where 2,903 servicemen are buried or commemorated.
And listen to the names. One ridge has three, Tunisian, British and German, each left by people who were there.
Five stops and some 500 kilometres, from the dunes to the gates of Tunis.
At each one, the ground helps you read the war, with a stone, a firing slit, a cliff edge, a date, or a name.
For the people who live here, these are not only battlefields. They are an oasis, a village, a garden and a valley.
Many soldiers who came here never went home. Their cemeteries are part of the trail too.
Check access locally, travel gently, and leave each place as you found it.
The war crossed Tunisia in six months. Its traces are still here, for anyone who knows how to look.
